settings.title: Shared settings
settings.hint: These values are used by both calculators.

solar.title: Solar plant payback
solar.exportSurplusLabel: Is surplus electricity exported to the grid?
solar.exportSurplusYes: Yes, surplus is exported and settled with ESO
solar.exportSurplusNoHint: With "no export" selected, no ESO settlement method applies: surplus electricity (beyond what's used instantly and any battery capacity) is simply unused, and any shortfall is bought from the grid at the full price.
solar.settlementSourceNote: These are the 4 official ESO (Lithuanian distribution operator) settlement methods for grid-connected prosumers, with 2026 prices approved by VERT (the energy regulator). You can only pick one method at a time (they cannot be combined), and can change it at most once every 12 months. Full details and official figures:
solar.settlementTariffPlansLinkText: ESO – transmission tariff plans and prices 2026
solar.settlementPerKwhFeeDesc: Every kWh you export to the grid can later be retrieved free of charge, but you pay this distribution fee for each kWh you retrieve (2026: €0.0726/kWh at low voltage). ESO recommends this method for new prosumers whose system is installed at the consumption site (e.g. on the house roof).
solar.settlementCapacityFeeDesc: Instead of a per-kWh fee, you pay a fixed monthly fee based on the *permitted export capacity* (kW) of your connection point, regardless of how much energy you actually retrieve from the grid. The 2026 rate is €5.0336/kW/month at low voltage. Important: if ESO has set an export power limit (e.g. 1 kW), the fee is based on that limit, not the full installed system capacity. ESO recommends this method for remote prosumers or anyone wanting a fixed, consumption-independent cost.
solar.settlementPercentageDesc: ESO keeps a fixed percentage of every kWh you export as payment for network usage, and the remainder becomes your usable energy credit (2026: ESO keeps 37%, so 63% remains as credit). ESO recommends this method for prosumers whose system generates more than ~130% of their consumption needs.
solar.settlementTariffManualDesc: The fee is set equal to your own electricity distribution/transmission tariff (depends on your supplier's tariff plan and voltage level). 2026 examples (low voltage, incl. VAT): single time-zone "Standartinis" plan - €0.11132/kWh; two-zone day/night rate - €0.12947/€0.07139 per kWh. Find your exact rate on your electricity bill or the ESO tariff-plans page linked below, and enter it here manually.
solar.hasExportPowerLimitLabel: ESO only allows exporting a limited power to the grid
solar.exportPowerLimitHint: ESO can permit each connection point to export less power to the grid than the installed system capacity (set individually - some get 1 kW, others 10 kW or more). Since the calculator has no hourly production data, the amount above the limit is estimated from a typical daily solar output curve: the lower the permitted power is relative to the system's capacity, the more of the surplus is lost (unused) rather than exported.
solar.exportPowerLimitOffHint: If you don't know of any restriction, or there isn't one, the calculator assumes all surplus power can be exported without limits.
solar.threePhaseSyncModeLabel: Three-phase synchronous inverter (export limited equally per phase)
solar.threePhaseSyncHint: With a synchronous 3-phase inverter the export limit is enforced per phase (limitKw ÷ 3). If load is concentrated on one phase (which absorbs its own solar locally), the unused export budget of that phase cannot be transferred to the other two — total effective export is at most 2/3 of the full limit. This only matters when the export limit is actually binding (i.e. limit < system capacity).
solar.expiredCreditCompensationHint: ESO pays a small compensation for kWh credits that expire unused after the 24-month banking window. This is roughly the electricity exchange (NordPool) spot price — approximately €0.03/kWh, though it varies. Set to 0 for a conservative estimate (no compensation).
solar.annualMaintenanceCostHint: A rough annual reserve for possible failures and maintenance: inverter replacement (typically needed every ~12-15 years), spread evenly over the years, plus minor repairs and panel cleaning. Just a starting estimate - real costs depend on system size and component quality/warranties.
solar.panelDegradationPctHint: Solar panel output gradually declines every year due to natural ageing. Most manufacturer warranties guarantee around 80-90% of the original output after 25 years, i.e. an average of ~0.4-0.6%/year - applied across every year of the calculation.
solar.hasBatteryLabel: I have / plan to have a battery (in the main scenario)
solar.batterySizingHint: The capacity and cost below are used not only for the main scenario (if the checkbox is on), but also for every battery variant in the "Comparison of all variants" section - even if the checkbox is off, so you can still see whether a battery would pay off.
solar.batteryCostHint: Rough market estimate for this capacity: ~{{estimate}} €. Real prices vary a lot depending on voltage class (low/high), manufacturer, and installation complexity - actual cost can be up to twice as much.
solar.batteryDegradationPctHint: Battery capacity fades every year from cycling and calendar ageing - usually faster than panel output decline. Typical LFP batteries retain about 70-80% of their original capacity after ~10 years (~2%/year). Applied across every year of the calculation.
solar.batteryUsableCapacityPctHint: Batteries are usually not charged to 100% or drained to 0% in practice (a BMS/manufacturer safety margin protects capacity) - e.g. charging to ~95% and reserving ~5-10% at the bottom means about 85-90% is actually usable. Lower this if you know your battery/inverter setup keeps a bigger reserve.
solar.daytimeConsumptionShareHint: What share of total consumption happens during solar production hours (daytime) - the rest is assumed to happen in the evening/night. This matters even without a battery: daytime surplus is exported into the settlement credit bank, while night consumption is bought from the grid - either from that credit (if any remains) or at the full price (once the credit is used up).
solar.resultsPaybackNever: Does not pay back within {{years}} years
solar.sectionMonthlyFlow: Monthly production, consumption and grid interaction
solar.sectionMonthlyFlowHint: "Production" below is the theoretical yield from irradiance and installed capacity, regardless of whether there's anywhere for it to go. A real inverter doesn't generate power "into nowhere": if the home doesn't consume it, the battery can't take it, and it can't be exported (or ESO's permitted export power limit is in the way), the inverter simply throttles its own output down to match what's needed - it never actually generates that extra energy, rather than generating and discarding it. So the "Unrealized potential" and "Unrealized potential from the export power limit" rows below represent energy that is simply never generated in reality, not electricity that's physically wasted after being produced. Each month is calculated in this order: (1) production is used instantly for self-consumption, up to that month's daytime load; (2) any remaining daytime surplus is charged into the battery, if there is one, limited by its size and by how much the following night can actually use; (3) the battery is discharged overnight to cover night-time load (with round-trip losses); (4) if surplus still remains after the battery, it is exported to the grid (unless export is disabled) - possibly clipped by ESO's permitted export power limit; (5) if there is no battery, or export is disabled, any remaining potential is simply never generated in reality; (6) any shortfall (production and battery together weren't enough) is covered either from previously banked (own, exported) kWh credit, or bought at the full retail price if the bank is empty. Because a summer day's surplus cannot be "shifted" to night without a battery, night-time purchases can look similar every month even when production varies a lot - but banked credit stays valid for 24 months from when it was produced, not wiped out on January 1st, so you don't always pay full price for it.
solar.flowCurtailedByExportLimit: Unrealized potential from the export power limit (not actually generated)
solar.flowExpiredCreditsCompensationNote: {{kwh}} of banking credits expired this year — ESO pays compensation for them ≈ {{eur}}/yr.
solar.flowRetainedByEso: Retained by ESO (percentage-method network fee, not entering the credit bank)
solar.assumptionBattery: The battery model uses monthly averages and the "daytime consumption share" set below (default ~35%, adjustable), assuming every day in the month is identical (a "typical day" repeated all month). It does not simulate actual hourly load, and it does not carry over an undischarged battery remainder from one real day to the next (e.g. after several cloudy days in a row) - that would require daily/hourly production data, which this calculator does not have. Results depend on your real daily profile (e.g. if you barely use any power at home during summer days, lower this share or increase battery capacity for a more realistic picture).
solar.assumptionCreditExpiry: Net-metering credit is not wiped out every January 1st - Lithuania uses a fixed 2-year accumulation cycle (starting 1 April of even years), approximated here as a rolling 24-month window from when each kWh was produced, redeemable any time within that window (oldest credit first). In reality, unused expired credit isn't simply lost - ESO/the supplier pays a cash compensation for it (0.02939 €/kWh for the 2024-2026 cycle); the calculator does not yet model this compensation, so unused credit's value is slightly understated here. Since 2026, 4 alternative ESO settlement methods apply - they are not combined with each other. The calculator does not model the changes expected from 2031.
solar.assumptionNoBatteryNoExport: Without a battery and without grid export: only the electricity used the instant it's produced counts, and any surplus is simply lost (unused, no payback for it), while the full monthly shortfall is bought from the grid at the full price.
solar.assumptionExportPowerLimit: The permitted export power limit is estimated with a simplified typical daily solar output curve (without hourly data, it's not possible to know exactly when during the day the limit is exceeded) - the actual amount lost depends on your system's and household's real daily profile.
solar.comparisonHint: Compares every ESO settlement method, with and without a battery, to help pick the best option. The best (highest net benefit) is highlighted.
solar.variantNonePerKwhFee: No battery - fee per kWh retrieved

heating.title: Firewood/pellets → heat pump + solar
heating.intro: Evaluate whether it's worth switching firewood/pellet heating to a heat pump, together with a solar system and battery - accounting for current fuel and electricity use, price growth, and total household electricity demand (including the heat pump in winter).
heating.fuelUnitHint: The unit depends on the selected fuel type: firewood is measured in stere (m³), pellets in kilograms (kg).
heating.energyContentHintFirewood: Depends on wood species and dryness: dry (~20% moisture, seasoned at least a year) birch/ash/hornbeam firewood is ~1700 kWh/m³, softwood (pine/spruce) ~1400-1500 kWh/m³, damp/green firewood - up to 30-40% less. Without more specific data, the default 1700 kWh/m³ is a reasonable estimate.
heating.energyContentHintPellets: Standard wood pellets (ENplus A1 grade) are ~4.6-4.9 kWh/kg - the value barely varies between manufacturers and is usually printed on the bag. Without bag data, the default 4.7 kWh/kg is a reasonable estimate.
heating.recommendedPowerKwHint: Calculated from your current annual heat demand - pick the closest power rating actually available on the market.
heating.householdSharedHint: This data is shared with the Solar tab - changing it here also changes it there.
heating.solarAssumptionsHint: Uses the assumptions set in the Solar tab (settlement method, price/kW, battery efficiency, etc.) - currently set to {{capacityKw}} kW, {{priceKw}} €/kW there. To change these assumptions, go to that tab.
heating.sectionRecommendation: Recommendation: solar capacity and battery size
heating.winterMismatchHint: The heat pump uses most of its electricity in winter, when the solar system produces the least - so solar only covers part of the heat pump's demand, and most of the benefit comes from saved fuel plus summer surplus export/storage.
heating.recommendationSummary: Best option by net benefit: a {{capacityKw}} kW solar system with a {{batteryKwh}} kWh battery.
heating.recommendationSummaryNoSolar: Best option by net benefit: heat pump only, no solar system.
heating.resultsPaybackNever: Does not pay back within 20 years
